The paper introduces the Enhanced Reduced Basis Method (EnRBM) for model-order reduction in hybrid electromagnetic analysis.
The method is applied to problems involving the Generalized Impedance Matrix (GIM).
The hybrid approach combines finite element method (FEM) and mode-matching (MM) techniques.
The GIM relates electric and magnetic fields on the boundary of a discrete region.
The EnRBM uses a projection basis formed from FEM solutions at selected frequencies.
The projection basis is expanded using a greedy algorithm based on error estimation.
A residual error-based estimator is used to guide the selection of new snapshot frequencies.
The error estimator is computed quickly and used to automate the reduction process.
Two test cases are analyzed: plane wave scattering from a cylindrical object and a periodic structure in a rectangular waveguide.
The scattering test case uses 201 equidistant frequency points in the band 9–11 GHz.
The periodic structure test case uses 501 frequency points in the band 9–17 GHz.
The projection basis for the scattering test case consists of 372 vectors over 6 frequency points.
The maximum estimated error in the scattering test case is 1.3e-03.
The real error in the far-field zone is much lower than the near-field error.
The proposed MOR method achieves a speed-up of up to 20.8 times compared to the standard hybrid method.
The speed-up increases with the number of frequency points.
The systems of equations are solved using MKL PARDISO and UMFPACK libraries.
The computational time for the full FEM with PML is 381.1 s (MKL PARDISO) and 405.2 s (UMFPACK).
The computational time for the hybrid method is 80.5 s (MKL PARDISO) and 301.1 s (UMFPACK).
The computational time for the hybrid method with MOR is 18.3 s (MKL PARDISO) and 24.5 s (UMFPACK).
The reduction process is fully automated in terms of accuracy.
The method is validated on both open and closed domain problems.
The error estimator is based on the interaction between the residual error and the right-hand side matrix.
The reduction process stops when the estimated error drops below a specified tolerance.
The method is suitable for both scalar and vector formulations.
